messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar is a 41-year-old married man who came to treatment after months of telling his wife that he was “fine” and then finding himself increasingly unable to move through ordinary parts of the day without a jolt of dread and shame. Before coming to the United States, he had lived as a civilian in a city repeatedly struck during the war. What remains most vivid to him is not a single clean scene but a cluster of moments: the crack and boom of incoming fire, the shouted names of neighbors as people searched through dust and confusion, and the heavy smell of churned soil and concrete after blasts tore open streets and courtyards. He remembers standing outside after one attack, dirt thrown up into the air, hearing someone call a familiar name again and again with no answer. Even now, when he talks about that period, he does so flatly, as if the feeling has drained out of the memory while the details remain painfully sharp.

In the years since, Omar has built a life around dance, teaching and rehearsing in a studio where music, bodies, and repetition usually give him structure. Yet the very texture of daily life keeps catching on what happened. A sudden percussive sound in rehearsal, a bass note that lands like an explosion, or construction noise from the street can make his body go rigid. If he passes a park after rain or steps near a planter outside the studio and catches the smell of wet earth, he is abruptly back in the aftermath of bombardment, with the ground itself feeling dangerous. Hearing certain Arabic names—especially when called loudly across a room—hits him in a similarly private, destabilizing way, as though the present moment has been pierced by voices from those chaotic searches after an attack.

These moments do not end with surprise. They quickly harden into the beliefs that now organize much of his inner life. When a sound or smell catches him off guard, Omar becomes certain that whatever happened to him is still visible on him, that other people in the studio can see it in his face and posture before he has said a word. He will look at his students and fellow dancers and think they must notice something broken, some mark that gives him away. In those same moments he feels abruptly hollowed out, “dead inside,” as he has put it, disturbed by how little warmth or comfort he can find even when the danger has passed. The triggers also pull him toward a bleak conviction that the world is fundamentally stripped of goodness—that people did not protect one another, that life can be shattered at any second, and that whatever faith he once had in people or in a higher order has been worn away beyond repair.

Because his work depends on presence and expressiveness, this has become painfully visible to him in the studio. During rehearsal, if a loud sound from the street breaks through the music, he may lose the thread of the choreography and retreat into mechanical correction, speaking to dancers in clipped, overcontrolled ways. If someone calls out a name that reminds him of the war, he can no longer stay inside the creative moment; instead he becomes preoccupied with how exposed he seems, convinced the room can read his history on him. The smell of dirt from potted plants in the lobby or from the sidewalk after rain can leave him emotionally blunted for the rest of the session, going through the motions while feeling absent from himself. Each episode seems to confirm what he has come to believe: that something essential in him has gone numb and that trust—in people, in life, in anything beyond bare survival—was lost there and never came back.

At home, his wife has experienced him as increasingly distant. He does not describe feeling sad so much as emptied out. He sits with her in silence, aware that she wants closeness, but privately convinced there is nothing alive in him to offer. When a name on television or in conversation echoes one from that time, he withdraws further, watching her face for signs that she can see where he has gone. He knows this fear is difficult to explain without sounding irrational, yet to him it feels obvious: trauma is not hidden, it radiates outward, and others must be able to detect it.

What finally brought Omar to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulating humiliation of feeling split off from his work and marriage. After freezing during a rehearsal when construction noise erupted outside and then spending the evening convinced his dancers had seen him unravel, he admitted to his wife that he was frightened by how dead he felt inside and by how completely he had lost faith that people, life, or God could hold anything safely. He comes to treatment wanting relief from the constant sense of exposure, but what he is most afraid of is that the emptiness is permanent and that the war has already told the deepest truth about the world.
